blogs.title: After Ciminelli and Kousisis: Fifth Circuit Revives ‘Finfluencer’ Pump-and-Dump Indictment Under § 1348
blogs.description: Analyzes the opinion’s core holding that a fraudulent-inducement theory—alleging deception to induce followers to part with money for securities—states a § 1348 offense without invoking the discredited right-to-control theory. Explains the court’s element-by-element approach to ‘scheme to defraud’ and ‘intent to defraud’ and the significance of reversing the district court’s dismissal.

blogs.title: No Net-Loss Needed: Profit Motive and the Intent Element in Securities Fraud
blogs.description: Explores the court’s reliance on Kousisis to reject a ‘no harm, no foul’ defense where victims received market-value securities. Unpacks why obtaining victims’ money can satisfy intent to defraud even absent net pecuniary loss, and considers implications for price-manipulation and pump-and-dump prosecutions.

blogs.title: Mail/Wire Fraud as a Template: What This Decision Means for § 1348 Jury Instructions
blogs.description: Examines the opinion’s explicit borrowing from mail and wire fraud doctrine (material misrepresentations, intent to deceive and obtain property) and how that will shape § 1348 charging language and jury instructions. Flags open questions on materiality, the ‘object’ of the scheme, and how to convey fraudulent inducement to juries.

blogs.title: From Tweets to Trades: First Amendment Boundaries for Social-Media Stock Promotion
blogs.description: Assesses how misstatements about trading positions and price targets fit within unprotected fraud versus protected opinion or puffery. Discusses doctrinal tension between speech rights and fraud liability in influencer-driven markets, and offers practical takeaways for disclosures and disclaimers that won’t cure knowing falsehoods.

blogs.title: Why Charge § 1348 (and § 1349) Instead of Rule 10b-5? DOJ Strategy in Online Manipulation Cases
blogs.description: Compares § 1348’s scheme-based framework to traditional § 10(b)/Rule 10b-5 theories. Evaluates mens rea, ‘in connection with’ language, conspiracy under § 1349, and aiding-and-abetting under § 2, and why prosecutors might prefer § 1348 for social-media pump-and-dump fact patterns.

blogs.title: Pleading After Ciminelli: Drafting Indictments That Allege Property Deprivation Without ‘Right to Control’
blogs.description: Offers a practitioner’s guide to post-Ciminelli charging: tying misstatements to the object of obtaining money, avoiding mere deprivation of economic information, and articulating how victims parted with property. Uses the indictment here as a model for surviving a Rule 12 motion.

blogs.title: The Next Wave: Criminal Liability for Meme-Stock and Crypto Promotion Post-Kousisis
blogs.description: Places the decision in the broader enforcement trend against online market manipulation. Considers parallel civil enforcement, the Fifth Circuit’s approach alongside the Seventh Circuit’s application of Kousisis, and risk factors that put promoters and ‘finfluencers’ in the criminal crosshairs.

blogs.title: Injury Without Loss? Sentencing and Restitution After Fraudulent Inducement
blogs.description: Probes the downstream consequences of recognizing fraud without net loss: how courts might calculate Guidelines ‘loss,’ restitution, and forfeiture in inducement cases where consideration changed hands. Identifies potential friction points and defense strategies on quantifying harm.
